name: Chimney
tagline: A village named after the last brick of an old dak bungalow
meta_description: Chimney near Kurseong: the 1839 dak bungalow chimney on the Old Military Road, forest walks to Bagora, homestays with meals and how to get there cheaply.
summary: Chimney is a small forest village about 8 km above Kurseong at roughly 2,200 m, on the road over Dow Hill to Bagora. It is named after a lone brick chimney, all that remains of a British dak bungalow built around 1839. Homestays charge about ₹1,200–1,800 per person with meals.

local_story.title: The bungalow that left only its chimney
paras: Before the Hill Cart Road and the railway, travellers to Darjeeling came up an older route that local people still call the Old Military Road, which climbed through the forest over the ridge above Kurseong. Along such roads the British built dak bungalows, simple rest houses where officers, mail runners and travellers could stop for the night. Local accounts date the bungalow here to about 1839, only a few years after the Company took the Darjeeling tract in 1835.

When the new cart road and then the railway took the traffic in the 1860s to 1880s, the old road lost its purpose and the bungalow fell into ruin. What survived was its brick chimney, about 7 m (23 ft) tall, standing alone in a clearing. The village that grew up around it took its name from that one object. Today the chimney stands in a small fenced park, and the forest road it once served is a quiet route for walkers between Dow Hill and Bagora.

did_you_know: The lone chimney is about 7 m (23 ft) high and is the only part left of a dak bungalow that local accounts date to around 1839.
The road through Chimney follows the Old Military Road, the route to Darjeeling used before the Hill Cart Road was built in the 1860s.
Chimney sits roughly 700 m above Kurseong bazaar, so it is usually 3–5 °C colder than the town on the same day.
intro: Chimney is the kind of place you find by walking. There is a cluster of houses, a few homestays, some vegetable plots, a small fenced park around the old chimney and a great deal of forest. At about 2,200 m it is noticeably colder than Kurseong, and on clear mornings it looks out over the folds of the hills towards the plains and, northwards, to the snows.

It suits travellers who want a night of silence: a homestay dinner, a bukhari stove, stars over the ridge. Days are for walking: down through Dow Hill to Kurseong, along the ridge to Bagora, or into the forest with a local guide. Come in spring for rhododendron and magnolia, and in autumn for the clearest views. There is little to buy, so bring what you need from Kurseong.
facts: Jio and Airtel patchy; often weak indoors
costs: Local guide for a forest walk, half day

highlights.title: The old chimney
highlights.text: A brick chimney about 7 m high standing alone in a small park, the last piece of a dak bungalow from about 1839. Read the sign, look at the brickwork and imagine the mail runners and officers who stopped here on the old road up to Darjeeling.

highlights.title: Forest road from Dow Hill
highlights.text: Walk over the ridge from the Dow Hill schools to Chimney in about 1.5–2 hours through quiet conifer and broadleaf forest. Mist often comes in after midday, so start early.

highlights.title: Ridge to Bagora
highlights.text: Continue along the ridge to Bagora, a village at a similar height with open slopes and long views. A good half-day walk out and back from a Chimney homestay.

highlights.title: Spring flowers
highlights.text: In March and April rhododendron and magnolia flower on the higher slopes around Chimney and Bagora, and the forest edge fills with small wild flowers.

highlights.title: A cold, quiet night
highlights.text: At about 2,200 m, Chimney is several degrees colder than Kurseong. Homestays light bukhari stoves in winter; the silence after dark, with no traffic and few lights, is the reason to stay.

how_to_reach.text: From Kurseong a taxi takes 20–30 minutes over Dow Hill and costs about ₹700–1,000. From Siliguri, a car direct to Chimney via Kurseong costs about ₹2,800–3,500.
A few local jeeps run between Kurseong and Bagora via Dow Hill and Chimney, mainly in the morning and late afternoon, for ₹40–70. Ask at the Kurseong stand the day before for timings.
Walk from Kurseong bazaar via Dow Hill in about 3–3.5 hours, climbing roughly 700 m. Walk up, sleep, and take a jeep down the next day.

where_to_stay: Stay in one of Chimney's family homestays, which offer simple rooms with dinner and breakfast for about ₹1,200–1,800 per person; ask for extra quilts and a heater or stove in winter. We do not list individual properties here because they change hands and names; ask your Kurseong driver or check recent traveller reviews. Bagora, a little further along the ridge, also has a few homestays. If you prefer a town hotel, stay in Kurseong and visit Chimney for the day.
tips: Bring warm clothes even in April and October; nights at 2,200 m drop near freezing in winter.
Carry snacks and cash from Kurseong; there are only small shops here.
Start forest walks before 9 am, before the mist rises.
Confirm that your homestay has hot water and power backup before you book in winter.
Respect the fenced chimney park; do not climb on the brickwork.

experiences.title: The 1839 chimney on the old road
experiences.image_query: Chimney Kurseong old brick chimney park
experiences.summary: See the lone brick chimney that gave the village its name, the last part of a dak bungalow that local accounts date to about 1839. A short stop, and a good story about how people reached Darjeeling before the railway.
body: Dak bungalows were the travel lodges of British India: plain rest houses at intervals on main roads where officials and travellers could sleep, eat and change horses or porters. The one at Chimney stood on the Old Military Road, the early route to Darjeeling that climbed over the ridge above Kurseong.

Local accounts say it was built around 1839. Once the Hill Cart Road opened in the 1860s and the railway in 1881, traffic moved below and the old road and its bungalow were abandoned. The building crumbled; the chimney, about 7 m tall, did not.
Today the chimney stands in a small fenced park with benches. Look at the old brick, then walk a little along the road either way to see how the route keeps to the ridge.

faqs.q: Why is the village called Chimney?
faqs.a: Because the most visible thing left from its past is a single brick chimney, about 7 m tall, from a British dak bungalow that local accounts date to around 1839. The rest of the building fell into ruin after the old road was abandoned, and the village took its name from what remained.

faqs.q: What was the Old Military Road?
faqs.a: It was the early road to Darjeeling, used before the Hill Cart Road was built in the 1860s. It climbed through the forest over the ridge above Kurseong, past places such as Dow Hill and Chimney. Today parts of its line are quiet local roads used by walkers and village jeeps.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee for the Chimney park?
faqs.a: It has been free or a very small fee in recent years, collected locally. The park is small and takes 15–30 minutes to see. Check current status before you travel, especially if you plan to arrive late in the day.

experiences.title: Ridge walk from Chimney to Bagora
experiences.summary: Walk along the high ridge from Chimney to the village of Bagora and back, through forest and open slopes at about 2,100–2,200 m. Easy gradients, long views on clear mornings, very few vehicles.
body: From the chimney park follow the road along the ridge towards Bagora. It is a quiet road, used by village jeeps and a few cars, and it stays near the crest for most of its length. The forest opens in places to give views over the Balason side and the folds of hills running down to the plains.
Bagora is a scattered ridge village with fields of potatoes, cabbages and other vegetables and a few homestays. Have tea there and walk back the same way, or arrange for a car to pick you up.
In spring rhododendrons flower on the higher slopes. Start early: by midday cloud often wraps the ridge, and in winter the wind is cold.

faqs.q: How long is the walk from Chimney to Bagora?
faqs.a: Plan on about 1.5–2 hours each way at an easy pace, or about 4 hours return with a tea stop. The road keeps close to the ridge, so there is little steep climbing. Check the exact distance with your homestay, as people measure it from different starting points.

faqs.q: Do I need a guide for the Bagora ridge walk?
faqs.a: No, the route follows a road. A local guide, about ₹800–1,200 for a half day, is useful for birds, plants and short forest paths off the road. Carry water, a jacket and a phone with offline maps, as signal is patchy.

faqs.q: Can I stay at Bagora instead of Chimney?
faqs.a: Yes. Bagora has a few village homestays at similar prices, about ₹1,200–1,800 per person with meals. It is slightly more remote. Some travellers stay one night in each and walk between them with their bags carried by car.

experiences.title: A homestay supper by the bukhari
experiences.summary: Eat a hill family's dinner beside a bukhari, the iron wood stove of Darjeeling winters: rice, dal, local greens, squash, perhaps chicken or pork, and pickles made in the house.
body: The bukhari is a small iron stove with a chimney pipe, fed with wood or coal, that heats the main room of many hill houses in winter. In a Chimney homestay it is where everyone gathers after dark, and dinner often comes to you there.

Expect rice, dal, a vegetable such as iskus (chayote squash), seasonal greens, potatoes from the ridge fields and a pickle of radish or chilli. In winter you might get gundruk, fermented leafy greens, in a sour soup. Meat dishes, chicken or pork, cost extra in some homes.
Ask your host about what they grow; most families on this ridge farm vegetables. Tell them in advance if you are vegetarian or do not eat certain things.

faqs.q: What food do Chimney homestays serve?
faqs.a: Home-style Nepali hill food: rice, dal, seasonal vegetables such as chayote squash and greens, potatoes, pickles and sometimes chicken or pork. Breakfast is often puri or roti with potato curry, or bread and eggs. Meals are usually included in the per-person rate.

faqs.q: Do homestays in Chimney have heating?
faqs.a: Many keep a bukhari wood stove in the main room and give heavy quilts. Some offer electric heaters, sometimes for a small extra charge. Ask before you book in December and January, when nights can approach freezing.

faqs.q: Can I get vegetarian food in Chimney?
faqs.a: Yes. Most hill homestay meals are vegetable-based anyway, with dal, rice and greens. Tell your host when you book so they can plan, and mention any allergies. Vegan diets are harder because ghee and dairy appear in many dishes.

experiences.title: Sunrise from the Chimney ridge
experiences.summary: Step out of your homestay before dawn and walk a few minutes to an open bend on the ridge. Watch light spread over layers of hills and valley mist, with snow peaks to the north on the clearest winter mornings.
body: Chimney's height, about 2,200 m, puts it above much of the morning mist that settles in the valleys. On a clear day between October and March, you can watch the sun rise over a sea of cloud with dark ridges sticking through it.

Ask your homestay host for the nearest open bend; the forest blocks the view in many places. Be out 20–30 minutes before sunrise and dress for the cold: it can be near freezing in December and January.
Views of the snow peaks to the north are possible but not guaranteed here; if Kanchenjunga is your priority, go to Ahaldara or Darjeeling's viewpoints. Chimney's gift is the light and the silence.

faqs.q: Can I see Kanchenjunga from Chimney?
faqs.a: Sometimes, from open bends on the ridge on very clear mornings in winter, but trees block much of the northern view. If seeing Kanchenjunga is important, plan a dawn at Ahaldara near Latpanchar or at Darjeeling. Chimney is better for sunrise over valley mist.

faqs.q: What time is sunrise near Kurseong?
faqs.a: Roughly 5 am in May and June and about 6.15 am in December and January. Be at your viewpoint 20–30 minutes earlier for the best light. Your homestay host can tell you the exact time and the nearest open spot.

faqs.q: Is it very cold at Chimney in winter?
faqs.a: Yes, for the hills. At about 2,200 m, December and January nights can drop close to freezing, and dawn on the ridge is windy. Bring thermals, gloves, a warm hat and a down jacket. Snow is rare but not unknown.

faqs.q: Where is Chimney village?
faqs.a: Chimney is about 8 km above Kurseong in Darjeeling district, on the road that climbs over Dow Hill towards Bagora. It sits at roughly 2,200 m. From Kurseong it takes 20–30 minutes by car or about 3 hours on foot.

faqs.q: Why is it called Chimney?
faqs.a: The village is named after a single brick chimney, about 7 m tall, the last part of a British dak bungalow that stood on the Old Military Road to Darjeeling. Local accounts date the bungalow to about 1839. The chimney now stands in a small park.

faqs.q: Is Chimney worth an overnight stay?
faqs.a: Yes, if you want quiet. There is not much to 'see' beyond the chimney, but a night here gives you forest walks, a cold clear sunrise and a homestay dinner with no traffic noise. For a busy sightseeing trip, visit for an hour from Kurseong instead.

faqs.q: How much does a homestay in Chimney cost?
faqs.a: About ₹1,200–1,800 per person per night with dinner and breakfast, as an indication for 2025–26. Rooms are simple, often with an attached bathroom. Ask about hot water, heating and power backup when you book, especially in winter.

faqs.q: How do I reach Chimney from Siliguri?
faqs.a: Take a shared jeep to Kurseong (₹150–200, 1.5–2 hours), then a local taxi to Chimney for about ₹700–1,000, or a local jeep towards Bagora if one is running. A reserved car from Siliguri to Chimney costs about ₹2,800–3,500.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Chimney?
faqs.a: October to December for clear mornings and dry forest walks, and March to May for rhododendrons and birdsong. Winter is cold but clear. July and August are very wet, with leeches and mist, and roads can be slippery.

faqs.q: Can I walk from Kurseong to Chimney?
faqs.a: Yes. Walk up from Kurseong bazaar through Dow Hill and over the ridge in about 3–3.5 hours, climbing roughly 700 m on a quiet road. Start by 8 am. Many walkers send bags by car and walk light.

faqs.q: Is Chimney good for families?
faqs.a: Yes for families who like walking and quiet. Children enjoy the chimney park and the forest, but there are no shops or play areas. Bring warm clothes and snacks, and confirm heating and hot water with your homestay.

faqs.q: Is there mobile network in Chimney?
faqs.a: Jio and Airtel work in places but signal is patchy, especially indoors and in the forest. Do not count on mobile data for work. Download offline maps before you leave Kurseong and tell your homestay host your plans for the day.
